title: Managing pain during childbirth
intro: Labour contractions are painful for most women, but pain varies widely between individuals. There are many ways to cope, from relaxation and movement to medicines and epidural anaesthesia. Learning about the options in advance helps you make choices that suit you, and you may change your mind during labour.

sections.heading: Why labour hurts
paragraphs: Pain arises from the strong contractions of the womb, the stretching of the cervix and birth canal and pressure on surrounding structures. It builds in waves and has pauses between contractions. Fear and tension can increase the experience of pain, which is why feeling safe and supported matters.

sections.heading: Non-medical methods
paragraphs: Many women find help in movement and changing positions, warm water or a birth pool, massage, breathing techniques, heat packs and having a supportive person present. Antenatal classes teach relaxation and breathing. Continuous support from a midwife or birth companion is linked to less need for medicines and greater satisfaction.
Other approaches such as TENS machines, hypnobirthing and acupuncture are used by some, with mixed evidence of benefit.

sections.heading: Medical pain relief
paragraphs: Options include nitrous oxide gas, which is inhaled during contractions and wears off quickly, and opioid injections, which reduce pain but can cause drowsiness and affect the baby's breathing. An epidural places a small tube near the spinal nerves to give continuous local anaesthetic and is the most effective pain relief. It can lengthen labour, lower blood pressure, and sometimes limit movement.
Spinal and combined techniques are also used, especially for Caesarean birth. Complications are uncommon but include headache, back soreness and incomplete pain relief.

sections.heading: Planning without rigid expectations
paragraphs: Write down your preferences but remain flexible. Labour can be unpredictable, and pain relief that is available differs between hospitals and birth centres. Ask in advance what is offered, how quickly an epidural can be arranged and what happens at home births.

sections.heading: After birth
paragraphs: Pain relief may continue after birth for stitches or Caesarean wounds. Talk to your midwife about how you feel about the experience, since difficult births can leave lasting distress.

examples.title: Making a birth plan
examples.text: Imagine you are expecting your first baby. You could talk with your midwife about breathing, movement and water, learn when and how to request an epidural, and discuss what you would like if labour changes direction.

examples.title: Involving your partner
examples.text: Suppose your partner will accompany you. You might practise massage and breathing together, and agree who will speak up to ask for help or advice.
